events.text: The light lets you go on a terrace of cloud, and three envoys are already waiting, the way crows wait. The one from {ln_order} reads a list, finds no name like yours, and reads it again to be sure. A second envoy asks which god sent you. None, you say. The third envoy writes that down as if it were a crime.

choices.text: Say your name again, slowly

effects.log: You say it twice. The envoy spells it wrong, and keeps it that way.

choices.text: Ask them what list they keep

effects.log: They do not answer, but one of them looks at you properly for the first time.

choices.text: Walk past them into the realm

effects.log: You go in unannounced. The crows talk about it for a month, which is a kind of fame.

events.text: Your first prayer arrives before your first friend does: a farmer on a world you never saw, asking for rain, addressed to nobody in particular. It lands on you because nobody else wanted it. {ln_elder}, passing on a road of star river light, sees the prayer in your hand and laughs. 'They send the newcomers the leftovers,' the old god says.

choices.text: Answer the farmer anyway

effects.log: Rain falls on one field, very carefully. Somewhere below, a farmer bows to the sky.

choices.text: Ask the old god where the good prayers go

effects.log: 'Up,' says {ln_elder}, and points at halls you cannot see yet.

choices.text: Drop the prayer back into the clouds

effects.log: It falls away unanswered. You feel lighter, and a little smaller.

events.text: The envoys of two pantheons meet you at once and size you up like a horse at fair, which is better than being ignored and worse than being welcomed. The envoy of {ln_order} feels the weight of your Dao and nods slowly. 'Sound enough,' the envoy says. 'For the Isles.' The other envoy pretends to have somewhere else to be.

choices.text: Thank the envoy for the half compliment

effects.log: You take the half and leave the rest. The envoy remembers that you did.

choices.text: Ask what 'for the Isles' is worth here

effects.log: 'About half,' says the envoy, honestly. You know where you stand, at least.

choices.text: Let your Dao press back, just once

effects.log: The envoy steps back a pace and pretends not to have. Now they both remember you.

events.text: {ln_peer} came through the light the same hour you did, and the envoys sort the two of you like fruit. {ln_peer} is taken to a hall with a door of morning; you are given a bench outside it and a cup of something cold. Nobody explains the difference. You suspect it is the colour of {ln_peer}'s robes and nothing more.

choices.text: Wait on the bench with good grace

effects.log: You wait a whole season. When the door opens for you, they notice you did not complain.

choices.text: Ask {ln_peer} what was said inside

effects.log: 'They asked who my teacher was,' says {ln_peer}. 'Then they stopped listening.'

choices.text: Leave the cold cup and find your own way in

effects.log: You find a side door. A god sweeping the floor of heaven nods you through.

events.text: Word of you came up the star river before you did. The envoys know {ln_was} has arrived, and they come in a crowd to look, the way gods look at a comet: with interest, and a polite certainty that it will burn out. {ln_elder} of {ln_order} says it aloud. 'Famous on the Isles. Here, the Isles are where our gardeners retire.'

choices.text: Laugh with them, not at yourself

effects.log: You laugh first, which spoils the joke for them. A few smile anyway.

choices.text: Remind them who you were

effects.log: You list it all. They listen, and nod, and you can see them file it under the Isles.

choices.text: Ask the old god about the gardeners

effects.log: 'Good gardeners,' says {ln_elder}, surprised. 'Better than most gods.' A strange start.

events.text: A herald announces you at the Heavenly Court's outer gate, reading from the scroll the Isles sent up: every title, every seat, every war you won. It takes a long time. When it is done, the gods in the gallery applaud the way one applauds a child who has recited something long. 'Next,' says the herald, and you are not next any more.

choices.text: Bow to the gallery as if it were sincere

effects.log: You bow deeply. The gallery is not sure whether it has been mocked, and likes you more for it.

choices.text: Ask the herald for the scroll back

effects.log: The herald hands it over. 'Keep it,' the herald says. 'It will matter again, later.'

choices.text: Tell the gallery the Isles are still listening

effects.log: You say it plainly. A few of the oldest gods stop smiling, and look at you instead.

events.text: At a feast of the gods you are seated behind a pillar, beside the table where the lesser domains keep their spare weather. {ln_elder} sends the wine to every seat but yours, not out of malice but because the servant was told the pillar is empty. When the toast is raised to the new age, you raise a cup of nothing.

choices.text: Raise the empty cup to the toast

effects.log: You raise nothing with great ceremony. The servant sees, and brings you a jug after.

choices.text: Move the pillar, politely

effects.log: You shift it a hand to the left. Now the whole hall can see you, and is not sure how to feel.

choices.text: Leave early and look at the stars

effects.log: You watch the star rivers alone. They do not seat anyone behind a pillar.

events.text: The Book of Fates keeps a page for every god. Yours, when you ask to see it, is a scrap pinned to the back with a note in a clerk's hand: 'Isles-born. Pending.' The archivist of {ln_order} apologises and does not mean it. 'Pages are for gods who have done something here,' the archivist says. 'Come back when you have.'

choices.text: Ask what counts as something

effects.log: 'Something we noticed,' says the archivist. It is the most useful thing you have been told.

choices.text: Write your own line on the scrap

effects.log: You add one line in your own hand. The archivist is scandalised, and does not rub it out.

choices.text: Thank the archivist and go to work

effects.log: You go out to do something worth a page. The scrap stays pinned, waiting.

events.text: Gods do not shout; they rearrange the light. When you walk into the Hall of Domains, the lamps along your side of the room dim one by one, a courtesy the old gods pay to guests they would like to see leave. {ln_peer}, who came up with you, has kept the brightest lamp by sitting under it and smiling at everyone.

choices.text: Sit in the dark as if you chose it

effects.log: You sit in the dark, perfectly at ease. By the end the lamps have crept back on their own.

choices.text: Light your own lamp

effects.log: Your own light, small and steady. Some gods find it rude. Others find it interesting.

choices.text: Ask {ln_peer} how the smiling is done

effects.log: 'You pretend you are already one of them,' says {ln_peer}. 'They hate to be the first to disagree.'

events.text: A god of small fortunes stops you on a road of cloud and asks you to carry a parcel to the far side of the realm. It is the errand they give to messengers. When you say you are a god, the god of small fortunes looks you over and says, 'Of course you are, dear,' and holds the parcel out a little longer.

choices.text: Carry the parcel; a god can be kind

effects.log: You carry it across the realm. The parcel holds a single lucky coin, which is now yours.

choices.text: Decline, and give your full title

effects.log: You give the whole title. The god of small fortunes writes it down so as to avoid you later.

choices.text: Carry it and say whose god you are

effects.log: At the far gate you sign for it with your own domain. The gatekeeper reads it twice.

events.text: Prayers rise past your door every night like lanterns on a river, and none of them stop. The worlds below do not know your name yet, and the gods who do know it are careful not to say it where mortals might overhear. {ln_elder} calls this keeping the river tidy. You call it a long, quiet night.

choices.text: Go down and let one world see you

effects.log: You show yourself to one village, briefly, in a cloud. They will tell this for three hundred years.

choices.text: Listen to every prayer that passes

effects.log: You learn what mortals want from gods, one lantern at a time. It is humbling.

choices.text: Ask {ln_elder} who decides the tidiness

effects.log: 'The ones with the most lanterns,' says {ln_elder}, and for once does not laugh.

events.text: You are invited to a council of {ln_order} at last, and given a seat, and a cushion, and a cup. Then the council speaks in the old tongue of the first gods, which nobody has used in ten thousand years except, it seems, today. {ln_elder} watches you over the rim of a cup to see whether you will pretend to follow.

choices.text: Pretend to follow, nodding wisely

effects.log: You nod at the right moments by luck. {ln_elder} narrows both eyes and says nothing.

choices.text: Ask for a translation, out loud

effects.log: The council stops. Then, grudgingly, it switches tongues. Several gods are relieved.

choices.text: Learn the old tongue from the words

effects.log: You listen until the shapes make sense. You leave knowing seven words of a dead language.

events.text: At the Divine Exchange, a stall keeper with a face like a polished coin serves the god beside you, then the god behind you, then a god who has not arrived yet and is still a rumour. 'Isles-born wait,' the keeper says when you ask. 'It is not personal. It is the order of things, and the order of things is very old.'

choices.text: Wait, and buy when served

effects.log: You wait out the rumour. When served, you are served well, out of a small embarrassment.

choices.text: Tell the keeper the order is about to change

effects.log: The keeper smiles politely. The gods in the queue remember the remark longer than the keeper does.

choices.text: Walk to a stall with no queue

effects.log: The empty stall sells odd things cheaply. You find a dream-cut whetstone for almost nothing.

events.text: The gods of the Elder Lineages hold their hunts on the moon, and newcomers are invited to carry the nets. {ln_peer} accepts at once and comes back with a story about a lineage heir who once carried nets too. You have been asked, as well, but the invitation was addressed to 'the one from the Isles' and spelled the Isles wrong.

choices.text: Carry the nets and watch the heirs

effects.log: You learn how the Elder Lineages hunt: slowly, together, and never for the meat.

choices.text: Correct the spelling and send it back

effects.log: Your corrected letter goes back up the moon. Someone there laughs, which is a start.

choices.text: Decline, and hunt alone that night

effects.log: You catch nothing, and see the moon from the side the heirs never visit.

events.text: The pantheon's gate asks a riddle before it opens, as it has asked every newcomer since the first sunrise: what can a god give that a god cannot take back? {ln_elder} waits beside it with an hourglass full of falling stars. The last newcomer answered 'mercy' and is still outside, thinking it over.

choices.text: Answer the riddle

ok.log: 'A name,' you say. The gate thinks, and opens. {ln_elder} turns the hourglass over, impressed.

fail.log: You answer, and the gate stays shut. {ln_elder} pats the stone kindly, as if it were you.

choices.text: Ask the gate what the last newcomer said wrong

effects.log: The gate is silent, but {ln_elder} is not: 'Nothing wrong. Only something easy.'

choices.text: Sit down beside the thinking newcomer

effects.log: You think together for a while. It is a good place to wait, outside a gate.

events.text: A hall of {ln_order} admits newcomers by the Test of the Mirror. You stand before a sheet of still water and it shows the gods what you are, not what you claim; most newcomers flinch and the water ripples, and that is the end of it. {ln_peer} went before you and the water froze over. Nobody is quite sure what that means.

choices.text: Stand still and let it look

ok.log: The water shows you plainly, and does not ripple. The judges write something down at last.

fail.log: The water ripples at one memory you did not expect. The judges write something down too.

choices.text: Refuse to be judged by water

effects.log: You walk away from the mirror. Some judges call it pride. One calls it sense.

choices.text: Ask {ln_peer} what the frozen water felt like

effects.log: 'Cold,' says {ln_peer}, 'and like being forgiven.' You decide to wait for another age.

events.text: The Throne of Storms tests newcomers in weather. You are given one cloud and asked to make it rain on a single field below without wetting the next one, while three thunder gods argue loudly about the seasoning of lightning. The field belongs to a widow who prays every morning. The next field belongs to her neighbour, who does not.

choices.text: Make the rain fall true

ok.log: Rain falls on one field only, a line drawn with water. The thunder gods stop arguing to look.

fail.log: The cloud drifts and both fields drink. The neighbour thanks the wrong god for it.

choices.text: Rain on both fields

effects.log: Both fields drink. You fail the test, and two families have a good year.

choices.text: Ask the thunder gods to keep it down

effects.log: They are so astonished they do. You still have to make it rain, but in peace.

events.text: The Silent Hall admits no one who cannot keep a secret, and its test is a secret. A judge with no face tells you something about {ln_elder} that would ruin that old god if it were known, then sends you out among the gods for a year. Every one of them, it seems, has been asked to find out what you were told.

choices.text: Keep it, all year, charmingly

ok.log: A year of questions and smiling answers about nothing. The faceless judge nods once.

fail.log: You keep the secret, but your face gives away that you have one. The judge sighs.

choices.text: Go to {ln_elder} and tell the old god first

effects.log: {ln_elder} listens, and says the secret was a lie. It was a test of something else.

choices.text: Refuse to carry a secret you were not asked to

effects.log: You hand it back unread. The Silent Hall cannot decide if that is wisdom or rudeness.

events.text: The Green Assembly tests a newcomer with a seed. Grow it, they say, and give no other instruction. {ln_elder} has been growing the same seed for six ages and it is still a seed, though a very respected one. You are given an hour, and a pot, and the attention of every old god in the garden.

choices.text: Grow it with patience

ok.log: The seed opens one green leaf, just one. The garden goes very quiet, then very warm.

fail.log: The seed stays a seed. {ln_elder} says this is normal, in a tone that makes it worse.

choices.text: Plant it in the ground, not the pot

effects.log: You plant it in open earth. They say nothing, but somebody waters it after you leave.

choices.text: Ask {ln_elder} about the old god's own seed

effects.log: You talk seeds for an hour. The test is forgotten by both of you, happily.

events.text: The Will of Heaven admits only gods who can be seen, and its test is to stand in the sun's own hall for a day without casting a shadow. Most newcomers burn a little, smile, and fail politely. {ln_peer} stood there yesterday and came out with a new and quieter voice. The door is held open for you now, gold and very hot.

choices.text: Stand in the hall and endure it

ok.log: You stand the whole day and cast no shadow. The hall decides, grudgingly, that you are seen.

fail.log: At noon your shadow slips out from under you. You come out sunburnt on the soul.

choices.text: Ask why being seen is the test

effects.log: 'Because a god nobody sees is a story,' says the doorkeeper. You think about that.

choices.text: Walk past the door; you came for other halls

effects.log: You go on. The Will of Heaven is not used to being walked past.

events.text: {ln_elder} stops you on the bridge over the star river with one hand raised. The old god has heard that the Isles call you strong and would like, as a matter of curiosity, to see how strong the Isles think strong is. 'One exchange,' {ln_elder} says. 'I will hold back. Do not take it personally when I win.'

choices.text: Take the exchange

roll.foeName: The old god on the bridge

ok.log: Your blow lands true. {ln_elder} stops holding back for a moment, then laughs and lets you pass.

fail.log: {ln_elder} does win, gently. You land on the far bank of the bridge, which is at least the right side.

choices.text: Bow and ask to be taught instead

effects.log: {ln_elder} considers. 'Cheeky,' the old god says, and teaches you one thing.

choices.text: Ask what the Isles think strong is

effects.log: 'Strong,' says {ln_elder}. 'That is the problem.' The hand comes down.

events.text: A god of war of {ln_order} has decided you are standing in the wrong place, which is any place the war god can see. 'The Isles send up their best,' the war god tells the courtyard, 'and we send them back.' Gods gather at the edges, the way weather gathers, to see whether they will be sending you back today.

choices.text: Meet the war god in the courtyard

ok.log: You are not sent back. The courtyard disperses, disappointed and very interested.

fail.log: You are sent back, a little: three courtyards over, into a fountain. The gods applaud the fountain.

choices.text: Step out of the place the war god can see

effects.log: You move one pace. The war god cannot find a reason, and looks foolish looking for one.

choices.text: Ask the war god which war it is

effects.log: 'Any war,' says the war god. 'Every war.' You leave with a better idea of this god than before.

events.text: At the Hall of Domains you are asked to hold your own domain for one turn of the hourglass while {ln_elder} leans on it. It is a custom, they say: old gods test the new gods' domains for weak walls. Your domain is small and new, and the old god's weight is the weight of a mountain range that remembers being sea.

choices.text: Hold the line

roll.foeName: The old god of the mountains

ok.log: Your domain holds. {ln_elder} lifts the weight off and grunts, which from that god is applause.

fail.log: Your wall gives a little. {ln_elder} steps back before it breaks, which is a mercy and a message.

choices.text: Open the domain and let the weight in

effects.log: You let it in and it finds nothing to break. {ln_elder} frowns, puzzled, then nods.

choices.text: Ask to lean on the old god in turn

effects.log: The hall laughs. {ln_elder} laughs loudest. 'Next age,' the old god says.

events.text: {ln_peer} has been challenged by a lineage heir of the Elder Lineages for sitting in a chair, and {ln_peer} cannot win. You were standing nearby, so now the heir has decided to challenge you as well, as a pair, for the convenience of the gallery. The chair was a very ordinary chair. Nobody was using it.

choices.text: Fight the heir beside {ln_peer}

ok.log: Two newcomers beat one heir. The gallery stops being convenient, and starts being very quiet.

fail.log: The heir wins, as heirs do. You both sit in the chair afterwards, out of spite, and nobody stops you.

choices.text: Offer the heir the chair

effects.log: You give the heir the chair. The heir has to sit in it, alone, with everyone watching.

choices.text: Pull {ln_peer} away before it starts

effects.log: You leave together. {ln_peer} sulks, but the next morning brings you tea.

events.text: A god of dreams of the Silent Hall challenges you to a duel in a dream, which is where that god cannot lose. The rules are simple: whoever wakes first loses. The gods of the Silent Hall have already started taking sides in silence, which is to say with looks, and none of the looks are on you.

choices.text: Enter the dream and stay asleep

ok.log: You sleep longer than the god of dreams. The god wakes, bewildered, in a room full of looks.

fail.log: You wake first, on the floor, to polite silence. Several gods have won something in it.

choices.text: Decline: you do not fight where you cannot see

effects.log: You decline. The dream god is relieved, and pretends to be offended.

choices.text: Agree, then simply never fall asleep

effects.log: You stay awake for a month. The god gives up first and calls it a draw.

events.text: The Throne of Storms settles a newcomer's place by thunder: two gods throw one lightning bolt each and the louder one keeps the seat. {ln_elder} has thrown first and the echo is still going round the mountain. You are handed a bolt that is still warm, and it is visibly smaller than the one {ln_elder} used.

choices.text: Throw the small bolt as hard as you can

roll.foeName: The thunder of the old god

ok.log: It is louder than it looks. The two echoes meet and argue, and yours is still going.

fail.log: A sharp crack and a long silence. {ln_elder} keeps the seat, and offers you the next one down.

choices.text: Hand the bolt back and keep standing

effects.log: You keep standing in the rain. In a pantheon of weather, that counts for something.

choices.text: Ask why louder means better

effects.log: 'It is the Throne of Storms,' says {ln_elder}. 'What else would it mean?' A fair point.

events.text: A god whose domain is Fortune challenges you to toss a coin made of a fallen star. Heads, you stay in the high gallery; tails, you go back to the bench. The coin has never once come up tails for this god, which {ln_peer} whispers to you is the whole point of having Fortune for a domain.

choices.text: Catch the coin in the air instead

ok.log: You catch the star coin before it lands. Fortune cannot rule on a coin that never fell.

fail.log: You miss. The coin lands heads for the god of Fortune, as it always has. You go back to the bench.

choices.text: Let it fall; take what Fortune gives

effects.log: It lands heads, for once in your favour. Even Fortune likes a gracious loser.

choices.text: Ask to toss the coin yourself

effects.log: The god of Fortune hesitates a long time. 'No,' the god says. Everyone hears the hesitation.

events.text: {ln_elder} has decided to put you in your place, and the place is the bottom stair of the Heavenly Court, where the sweepers sit. 'You may climb the stairs,' the old god says, 'one at a time, past me.' Each stair has an old god on it, and every one of them was once told the same thing by someone older still.

choices.text: Climb, one god at a time

roll.foeName: The old gods of the stair

ok.log: You climb six stairs before the seventh god stops you. Nobody newer has climbed four.

fail.log: The first god on the first stair is enough. You sit down among the sweepers, who make room kindly.

choices.text: Sit with the sweepers and listen

effects.log: The sweepers of heaven know every god by their dust. You learn a great deal.

choices.text: Ask the old god who told {ln_elder} the same

effects.log: The old god goes quiet, then names a god nobody remembers. You leave it there.

events.text: A herald of {ln_order} reads the record the Isles sent up after you. It says you were {ln_was}, and the herald reads it the way one reads a bill from a cheap inn: carefully, to see if one has been overcharged. 'A seat,' the herald says. 'On the Isles. How charming.' Someone in the back asks what an Isle is.

choices.text: Explain the Isles to the back of the room

effects.log: You describe the Isles so well that the back of the room goes quiet and homesick.

choices.text: Let the seat go; you are here now

effects.log: You let it go. A seat is a chair, and the chair is far below.

choices.text: Name the seat, and what it cost you

effects.log: You tell them what it cost. The herald stops sounding amused, and rolls the record up gently.

events.text: An immortal from the Isles who once knelt before {ln_was} has been raised here as a servant of a minor god, and recognises you in the Hall of Domains. Out of old habit, the servant bows to you, deeply, in front of everyone. The minor god is furious; the hall is delighted; you are, for one moment, two people at once.

choices.text: Raise the servant up and bow back

effects.log: You bow back as deep. The hall stops being delighted and starts being thoughtful.

choices.text: Accept the bow, as you once would

effects.log: You accept it. The minor god will not forgive this, and the hall will not forget it.

choices.text: Take the servant aside and ask after the Isles

effects.log: You talk for an hour about people you both knew. Some of them are gods now. Most are not.

events.text: The Book of Fates knows what you did on the Isles, all of it, and the gods have been reading over each other's shoulders. You were {ln_was}, and the gods who find this out do not lower their voices; they lower their eyes, which is worse. {ln_elder} alone looks straight at you. 'Well,' the old god says. 'Go on, then. Explain it.'

choices.text: Explain it, all of it, without excuse

effects.log: {ln_elder} listens to the end, and says only: everyone up here did something.

choices.text: Refuse to explain to anyone

effects.log: You refuse. The gods keep their eyes lowered, and a few start to look a little afraid.

choices.text: Ask what {ln_elder} once did

effects.log: 'Ah,' says {ln_elder}, and sits down. It is a long story, and not a nice one.

events.text: A small world below still prays against you, by name, as {ln_was}. The prayers rise every night past the halls of the gods and every god can read them, the way neighbours can read a letter held up to the window. {ln_peer} reads one aloud by accident at dinner, and then very much wishes not to have.

choices.text: Go down and answer them yourself

effects.log: You go down and stand in their square, and let them say it to your face. It changes something.

choices.text: Let the prayers rise; they are true

effects.log: You let them rise. Being cursed honestly is a strange kind of honour among gods.

choices.text: Tell {ln_peer} it is all right

effects.log: 'It is not all right,' says {ln_peer}. 'But thank you.' You share the rest of dinner in quiet.

events.text: Someone has hung a painting of you in the gallery of {ln_order}, a gift from the Isles, showing you as {ln_was}. The painter has made you taller and the gods find this very funny. They stand in front of it and look from the painting to you, and back, and something passes between them that is not quite respect.

choices.text: Stand beside it and match its pose

effects.log: You strike the same pose. The gallery laughs with you this time, not at you.

choices.text: Have it taken down

effects.log: It comes down. Some gods think it modest. Others think something to hide.

choices.text: Ask which god in the gallery painted their own

effects.log: A silence. Three of the oldest portraits suddenly need cleaning.

events.text: You were {ln_was}, and up here nobody knows, and nobody asks. {ln_elder} finds you on the edge of a cloud looking down toward the Isles, and sits beside you without asking either. 'Being nobody twice,' the old god says, 'is very good practice. Most of us only managed it once. Some of us keep wishing for it back.'

choices.text: Ask the old god what being somebody is like

effects.log: 'Loud,' says {ln_elder}. 'And full of letters.' You both look down for a while.

choices.text: Say that nobody is a fine thing to be

effects.log: {ln_elder} looks at you oddly, then nods. 'Keep that,' the old god says.

choices.text: Say you do not mean to stay nobody

effects.log: 'Good,' says {ln_elder}, and leaves. It sounded like a promise to watch.

events.text: {ln_order} gives every newcomer the same first labour: sweep the star river of dead light for a season. The dead light is heavy and does not want to be swept, and the river is long, and {ln_peer} was given the same broom last age and has not been seen since. Possibly {ln_peer} is still out there, sweeping.

choices.text: Sweep the river, the whole season

effects.log: You sweep a season of dead light into the dark. The river runs clearer behind you.

choices.text: Go looking for {ln_peer} with the broom

effects.log: You find {ln_peer} at the far end, still sweeping. You finish the labour together.

choices.text: Refuse a labour meant for servants

effects.log: {ln_elder} notes the refusal in pencil. The pencil, it seems, is very sharp.

events.text: The second labour of {ln_order} is to answer every prayer that lands in the pantheon's lost-and-found, a deep cloud where prayers go when they are addressed to gods who have died or changed their names. There are millions. Most are very small. One is from a child asking whether a dead dog is somewhere warm.

choices.text: Answer every prayer, starting with the child

effects.log: You answer the child first: yes, somewhere warm. Then the next million, one by one.

choices.text: Answer the small ones in great handfuls

effects.log: You answer them in batches. It is done, and nobody below notices the shortcut except you.

choices.text: Answer only the child, and leave the rest

effects.log: One prayer answered well. The labour is not done, and you are not sorry.

events.text: A domain of {ln_order} has gone quiet: a god of the Harvest fell asleep a thousand years ago and the fields below have learned to grow without anyone. Your labour is to wake the god without frightening the fields. {ln_elder} warns you that the last newcomer who tried it woke the fields instead, and they are still upset.

choices.text: Wake the god with a harvest song

effects.log: The Harvest god yawns, stretches, and asks what age it is. The fields go on growing, calm.

choices.text: Leave a note for when the god wakes

effects.log: A note in the god's ear: you were here, the fields were well. It counts, barely.

choices.text: Let the god sleep; the fields are fine

effects.log: You report back that nothing needs waking. {ln_elder} cannot decide whether you failed.

events.text: The labour is to carry the pantheon's lamp across the Hall of Domains during a quarrel of the old gods, without letting it go out and without taking a side. The old gods are arguing about the boundary between Death and Dreams, which has been argued for nine ages. Each side would very much like the lamp to tilt its way.

choices.text: Carry it straight down the middle

effects.log: You walk the whole hall with the flame upright. Both sides call it bias. It stays lit.

choices.text: Carry it, and speak for the dreamers

effects.log: The flame holds, and you speak once, for the dreamers. The labour counts; the Death gods remember.

choices.text: Set the lamp down and leave them to it

effects.log: {ln_elder} picks it up after you go. 'Not yet,' the old god says to no one.

events.text: {ln_order} sends you down to a small world below to put out a false god: a spirit of a river that has started demanding offerings and calling itself divine. The spirit is very small, very frightened, and has three villages praying to it who do not know it has never answered a single prayer.

choices.text: Unmask the spirit before the villages

effects.log: You show the villages a frightened little river. They laugh, then they forgive it. Labour done.

choices.text: Take the spirit into service and answer for it

effects.log: You teach it to answer prayers. It counts as putting out a false god: now it is a true one.

choices.text: Leave the spirit be; it harms no one

effects.log: You report the spirit harmless. The pantheon disagrees, and says so in ink.

events.text: The last labour is the dullest: copy out one page of the Book of Fates by hand, every word, for the pantheon's own library. The page is about a mortal who will live a long ordinary life, and it is very long and very ordinary. {ln_peer} copied a page last age and wept at the end of it, and would not say why.

choices.text: Copy it, every ordinary word

effects.log: You copy the whole life. At the end you understand why {ln_peer} wept.

choices.text: Copy it, and add a small mercy in the margin

effects.log: A clerk finds the margin and leaves it. The page is done, and one ordinary life a little kinder.

choices.text: Ask why gods copy what is already written

effects.log: 'So that we read it,' says {ln_elder}. It is not the labour, but it is an answer.

events.text: You come out of the College's examination hall into the realm's long afternoon. Three gods have read your answers on the nature of the Dao and the weight of a prayer. Pass or not, you said what you think, in a room that has heard everything already. {ln_peer} is waiting outside with two cups, one for each outcome.

choices.text: Take the cup for the good outcome

effects.log: {ln_peer} laughs. You drink to an answer you do not know yet.

choices.text: Ask for the other cup, just in case

effects.log: It is stronger. You drink it slowly, and feel better about everything.

choices.text: Walk back in and ask one more question

effects.log: The examiners are startled. One answers you, off the record. It is worth more than the exam.

events.text: The examination of the College is over, and you are not sure what it tested. They asked you only one question in the end, after all the reading, and it was a mortal's question: what do you do when nobody prays to you? You answered honestly. On the road out, a single prayer lands on your sleeve, quite by accident.

choices.text: Answer it at once

effects.log: You answer the accidental prayer. Somewhere a lost key is found, and somebody is very glad.

choices.text: Keep it, as a sign

effects.log: You keep the little prayer folded in your sleeve. Signs are rare even for gods.

choices.text: Think over your answer again

effects.log: You turn it over all the way home. Your Dao settles a little deeper.

events.text: After the College's examination you sit on the steps of its hall with other gods who sat it too, some old, some newer than you. Nobody talks about the questions. A god of the Sea who failed it four times tells a story about a whale instead, and then a god of Fate who passed it the first time tells a better one, about the same whale.

choices.text: Tell a story about the Isles

effects.log: You tell one. Nobody on the steps has heard it before. That is rare up here.

choices.text: Ask about the whale

effects.log: The two gods argue about the whale till sunset. You learn about both of them.

choices.text: Listen, and say nothing

effects.log: You listen. On the steps of a hard exam, gods are almost like people.

events.text: {npc} came through the light with you, and the gods treat {him} like luggage. At a banquet {npc} is seated with the servants of the minor domains, and a goddess of {ln_order} asks {him}, kindly, how long consorts of upstart gods usually last. {npc} smiles and says nothing, and you can see {him} counting the courses until it is over.

choices.text: Cross the hall and sit beside {npc}

effects.log: You move to the servants' table and stay. The goddess finds it hard to look at either of you.

choices.text: Answer the goddess, for {npc}

effects.log: 'As long as the gods who ask,' you say. The hall hears it, and so does {npc}.

choices.text: Let {npc} handle it, and ask later

effects.log: Later, {npc} says {he} has been looked down on before. {He} is not sure {he} minds less here.

events.text: {npc} has made a friend up here at last: a minor god of the Sea who talks to {him} about tides. Then the Sea god learns whose consort {npc} is, an upstart from the Isles, and stops coming. {npc} does not complain. {He} just goes to the shore of the star river every evening anyway, alone, and watches the tide come in.

choices.text: Go to the Sea god and stand for {npc}

effects.log: You go and say whose consort {npc} is, and what {he} is worth. The Sea god comes back.

choices.text: Walk the shore with {npc}

effects.log: You watch the tide together. It is enough for one evening, and {npc} says so.

choices.text: Tell {npc} the gods are not worth it

effects.log: {npc} looks at you a long time. 'You are a god,' {he} says. You let that sit.

events.text: {npc} is of your blood and followed you through the light, and the gods have decided this is what upstart gods do: bring their whole house up to fill the halls. A herald of {ln_order} turns {npc} away at a door of the Heavenly Court, politely, saying that kin of new gods wait in the outer garden until called. Nobody calls.

choices.text: Walk {npc} in through the door yourself

effects.log: You walk {npc} through the door, arm in arm. The herald pretends to be reading.

choices.text: Sit in the outer garden with {npc}

effects.log: You wait together. The garden, it turns out, is where the interesting gods sit anyway.

choices.text: Tell {npc} to make {his} own name

effects.log: {npc} nods slowly. {He} will. You can see it will take a long time.

events.text: {npc} has been answering prayers in your name while you were away, and doing it well, and a god of the Elder Lineages has filed a complaint: kin of upstart gods may not touch prayers. The complaint is read aloud at court. {npc} stands there with {his} hands still full of answered prayers, and does not know where to put them.

choices.text: Stand up and claim the prayers as yours

effects.log: You say {npc} answered them in your name, and well. The complaint is withdrawn, grudgingly.

choices.text: Take the prayers from {npc} quietly

effects.log: You take them so {npc} does not have to stand there. {He} thanks you, a little hurt.

choices.text: Tell {npc} to keep answering

effects.log: {npc} keeps answering, and the complaint stays filed. Some mortals below are very grateful.

events.text: {npc}, the student you raised on the Isles, came up through the light by {his} own strength and arrived to find {he} is known only as the student of an upstart god. The gods of {ln_order} turn {him} down for a minor domain {he} has every right to, saying the teacher is not yet anyone, so the student cannot be either.

choices.text: Go before the gods and vouch for {npc}

effects.log: You speak for {npc}: what {he} learned, and what {he} did. The domain is reconsidered.

choices.text: Tell {npc} to go to another pantheon

effects.log: {npc} looks hurt, then thoughtful. 'Another pantheon might not know your name,' {he} says.

choices.text: Teach {npc} one more thing, here and now

effects.log: You teach {npc} on a cloud, while the gods watch. It is the best lesson you have given.

events.text: {npc} has been challenged by a young god of War who wants to know what an upstart's student is worth. {npc} is worth a good deal, but is tired, and new to heaven, and the young god has chosen the hour carefully. Half the Hall of Domains has turned up to see the student lose, and to see how the teacher takes it.

choices.text: Step in: the student is under your word

effects.log: You stand beside {npc}. 'Under my word,' you say. The young war god finds another hour.

choices.text: Let {npc} fight; you watch

effects.log: {npc} fights, and loses well. Afterwards three gods ask {him} who taught {him}. {He} tells them.

choices.text: Ask the young god to fight you instead

effects.log: The young god of War looks at you, and finds a reason to leave.

events.text: {npc}, whom you met on the Isles and brought up through the light out of friendship, is being called the upstart's hanger-on by the gods of {ln_order}. It sticks the way such names do. {npc} has started to walk a little behind you in public, instead of beside you, and has stopped laughing at your jokes in front of others.

choices.text: Take {npc} by the arm and walk side by side

effects.log: You walk the length of the Hall of Domains together. The name begins to lose its grip.

choices.text: Tell {npc} it does not matter what they say

effects.log: 'It matters to me,' says {npc}. You walk on, a little apart, still friends.

choices.text: Find {npc} a work of {his} own up here

effects.log: You find {npc} work with the star river sweepers. {He} is good at it, and proud.

events.text: {npc} came up with you and has been treated by the gods as a sort of pet: patted, fed sweets, asked to tell stories of the Isles for laughs. {npc} is very good at the stories, and has started to change them so the gods laugh more. Tonight {npc} told one about you, and made you the joke, and the gods laughed hardest at that one.

choices.text: Laugh too, and then vouch for {npc} as a guest

effects.log: You laugh, then seat {npc} as your guest of honour. The gods stop patting {him}.

choices.text: Ask {npc} quietly why

effects.log: 'Because they like it,' {npc} says. 'Because it is safe.' You both sit with that.

choices.text: Tell a better story about {npc}

effects.log: You tell one about {npc} at {his} bravest. The gods do not laugh, and {npc} is quiet a long time.

events.text: A new god comes through the light this morning, a nervous one, and the envoys go to size the newcomer up. You realise, halfway through breakfast, that nobody has looked at you that way in an age. {ln_elder} passes your table and nods to you as one god nods to another, and does not stop to explain the custom of the nod.

choices.text: Go and meet the newcomer at the gate

effects.log: You stand beside the nervous god while the envoys circle. You know how it feels.

choices.text: Nod back to {ln_elder}, and finish breakfast

effects.log: You nod back. Breakfast is very good, now you taste it.

choices.text: Ask {ln_elder} when it changed

effects.log: 'When we stopped noticing,' says {ln_elder}. 'That is how it always changes.'

events.text: The Book of Fates has given you a whole page at last. Your scrap has been unpinned from the back and your name is written properly at the top, in the same ink as the others. {ln_peer}, who came up with you, has a page too, two shelves down. You stand together in the archive reading your own pages like strangers' letters.

choices.text: Read {ln_peer} your first line

effects.log: You read it aloud. {ln_peer} laughs, and reads you theirs. It is a good afternoon.

choices.text: Turn to the next blank page

effects.log: You look at the blank space that is still to come. It does not frighten you.

choices.text: Find the old scrap and keep it

effects.log: The scrap is in a drawer. You take it with you, the first thing heaven wrote about you.

events.text: At the feast for the new age you are seated in the light, not behind the pillar, and the wine comes to you without being asked. Someone has put a newcomer behind the pillar instead. The newcomer raises an empty cup to the toast, the way you once did, and catches your eye across the hall.

choices.text: Send the newcomer your jug

effects.log: You send the jug across the hall. The newcomer drinks the toast properly this time.

choices.text: Raise your own cup to the newcomer

effects.log: You raise it to the pillar. A few gods notice, and some remember.

choices.text: Go and sit behind the pillar yourself

effects.log: You sit down beside the newcomer. The hall is not sure what to do about it.

events.text: At the Divine Exchange the stall keeper sees no pantheon's seal on your sleeve and adds a quarter to the price of a jar of dream ink, in front of you, quite openly, with a little flourish of the brush. 'Gods with no pantheon,' the keeper explains, 'are a risk. Nobody stands behind the debt.' The god in line behind you nods.

choices.text: Pay the quarter more

effects.log: You pay. The keeper wraps the ink nicely, which is a sort of apology.

choices.text: Walk away without the ink

effects.log: You leave the jar on the stall. Your dreams will have to be written in plainer ink.

choices.text: Ask who stands behind the keeper

effects.log: The keeper goes pale. 'The Exchange,' the keeper says. You both know that is not an answer.

events.text: The Hall of the Sea holds its council open to every god of the waters, and you have been a god of rain on many small worlds. The door, when you reach it, is shut. A doorkeeper of {ln_order} explains through the grille that the council is open to every god of the waters who belongs to somebody.

choices.text: Wait outside and listen through the grille

effects.log: You hear the whole council through the grille. It is mostly about tides you could have helped with.

choices.text: Tell the doorkeeper you belong to the rain

effects.log: 'The rain is not a pantheon,' says the doorkeeper. 'It might be,' you say, and go.

choices.text: Go and hold your own council on a cloud

effects.log: You and two small river gods hold a council on a cloud. It is short, but it decides something.

events.text: A lesser god of a lesser domain, Lost Gloves, sneers at you in the road. Even Lost Gloves has a pantheon, a minor one, and wears its seal on a ribbon. 'At least someone wants me,' says the god of Lost Gloves, loud enough for a passing herald to hear, and adjusts the ribbon very carefully so you can see it.

choices.text: Compliment the ribbon sincerely

effects.log: The god of Lost Gloves is undone by sincerity and walks off confused.

choices.text: Remind the god what you were before

effects.log: You say it once. The god of Lost Gloves goes quiet. The herald hears that too.

choices.text: Ask the god what being wanted is like

effects.log: 'Tiring,' the god admits, all at once. It is the truest thing anybody has said to you here.

events.text: A tiny world at the edge of the star rivers, where the gods of the pantheons never go because the offerings are too small, has started praying to you. Not to a pantheon: to you, by a name they invented, which is almost right. The offerings are a bowl of rice and a song. It is the most faith anyone has sent you yet.

choices.text: Answer the tiny world in person

effects.log: You go down and stand in their festival. The children are not afraid. You stay three days.

choices.text: Correct the name, gently, in a dream

effects.log: You whisper the right name in one dreamer's ear. Next year the prayers are perfect.

choices.text: Keep the wrong name; it is theirs

effects.log: You keep it. A god can have two names. One is for a tiny world only.

events.text: You need a scroll of old weather-law from the Divine Exchange's archive, and the archivist charges every god the same fee, except that every god is in a pantheon, and so the fee for you, she says, has a rider. The rider is a quarter more, written in red. She shows it to you so you know it is not personal.

choices.text: Pay the rider

effects.log: You pay it. The scroll is old, the law is older, and both are worth knowing.

choices.text: Read the scroll in the reading room for free

effects.log: You read it standing up, all day. You leave with sore feet and the whole of it.

choices.text: Ask the archivist who wrote the rider

effects.log: 'An old god of {ln_order},' she says, 'who wanted to keep the archive tidy.'

events.text: The College of the Deep Dao turns you away from a lecture on the boundary between Fate and Luck, which you have spent three ages thinking about. A porter shows you the garden instead, very politely, and the gate behind the garden. {ln_peer} is inside, waves through the window, and looks a little guilty about it.

choices.text: Sit in the garden and think it through alone

effects.log: You think about Fate and Luck in a garden all afternoon. You get further than the lecture did.

choices.text: Ask {ln_peer} to tell you everything after

effects.log: {ln_peer} tells you all of it, word for word, over a cup. Friends are a back door.

choices.text: Climb the garden wall, quietly

effects.log: You hear half the lecture from the wall. The porter pretends not to see.

events.text: A god of a pantheon has offered to stand behind you, for a price: you would bow at {ln_order}'s feasts and send a tenth of the faith that rises to you. 'No backing, no table,' the god says. 'Every masterless god learns it in the end.' It is said kindly. That is what makes it heavy.

choices.text: Thank the god and refuse

effects.log: You refuse. The god shrugs and says the offer stays open. Offers like that always do.

choices.text: Ask what a tenth of faith buys

effects.log: 'A seat,' says the god. 'Not a voice.' You go home thinking about the difference.

choices.text: Say you would rather eat standing up

effects.log: The god laughs, and repeats it at a feast. Some of the gods there like it.

events.text: At a festival of the gods, every pantheon has a pavilion and every pavilion has a lantern. You have no pavilion, so you have no lantern, and the festival rule is that gods without a lantern may watch but not dance. A herald enforces this with great sadness. The music is very good and quite near.

choices.text: Watch from the edge, and enjoy it

effects.log: You watch all night. The music is still very good from the edge.

choices.text: Make your own lantern out of a star

effects.log: You hang a small star on a stick. The herald thinks about it, and lets you dance.

choices.text: Dance outside the festival, alone

effects.log: You dance where the music still reaches. A few minor gods come out to join you.

events.text: The Divine Exchange sells passage on the long barges of the star river, and the ferryman charges a god with no pantheon a quarter more, because, he says, a god with no pantheon might fall overboard with nobody to pull them out. The ferryman's assistant, a very young god, looks at the floor while he explains.

choices.text: Pay the quarter and ride

effects.log: You pay and ride. The young assistant brings you a blanket without being asked.

choices.text: Walk the star river bank instead

effects.log: It takes a month. You see things the barge never shows anyone.

choices.text: Ask the young assistant to sit with you

effects.log: You talk all the way to the next landing. The assistant has never met a masterless god before.

events.text: {ln_elder} of {ln_order} gives a reception for every god of a certain standing in the realm, and the list is read at the door. Your name is on it, crossed out, with a note in the margin: 'No backing. Later, perhaps.' The doorkeeper shows you the crossing-out, as a courtesy. It is very neat.

choices.text: Thank the doorkeeper and go home

effects.log: You go home. Later you hear that the reception was dull. You believe it.

choices.text: Write your own name back in, beside it

effects.log: You write it in, neatly. {ln_elder} sees it next morning and does not cross it out again.

choices.text: Send {ln_elder} a gift anyway

effects.log: A small gift of rain, very good rain. The old god sends a thank-you, and nothing else.

events.text: At the Divine Exchange, a craftsman god who shapes the forms gods wear sells you a new face for festivals, and adds a quarter to the price because, the craftsman says, a masterless god's face goes out of fashion faster. You suspect this is a story. You suspect, also, that it might be true.

choices.text: Buy the face, at the price

effects.log: You pay. It is a good face, and it does not go out of fashion for a long while.

choices.text: Keep your own face

effects.log: You keep your own. It is the one the small worlds pray to, after all.

choices.text: Ask the craftsman to make you one for free, as practice

effects.log: The craftsman is so surprised that one is made, slightly crooked, and sent with a note.

events.text: A small world in a far star river has been sending its prayers to the Will of Heaven for a thousand years and getting no answer. Now, in despair, it has started praying to 'whoever is listening'. You are listening. The Will of Heaven is not, and will be annoyed if anyone else answers the prayers it has been ignoring.

choices.text: Answer the far world openly

effects.log: You answer every prayer. The far world rejoices. The Will of Heaven notices, and says nothing yet.

choices.text: Answer quietly, in their dreams

effects.log: You answer in dreams so nobody high up can see. The world below sleeps better.

choices.text: Leave the prayers for their own god

effects.log: You leave them. That night the prayers rise past your door, still asking.

events.text: On the first day you call yourself a masterless god, a prayer arrives with your real name on it. It comes from Lantern Hollow, a little world at the end of a cold star river, where a shepherd named Oyun has found your name in an old story of the Isles. The flocks are dying of a sickness no god of the Harvest will look at. Lantern Hollow is too small to be anyone's.

choices.text: Go down to Lantern Hollow

effects.log: You walk into Oyun's pasture out of a cloud. The sickness is real, and so are you now.

choices.text: Send a blessing from above

effects.log: Your blessing reaches the flocks thinly. Oyun prays again next morning, with your name.

choices.text: Ask a Harvest god to look

effects.log: The Harvest god says Lantern Hollow is not in any pantheon's ledger. The prayer stays with you.

events.text: You take the sickness of Lantern Hollow to the pantheons, one after another, as a god with no pantheon may: by waiting in their outer gardens. Each pantheon thanks you, and asks which pantheon Lantern Hollow pays its offerings to, and on hearing none, discovers it has an urgent council somewhere else. Oyun keeps praying.

choices.text: Wait in one more garden

effects.log: {ln_elder} of {ln_order} finally sees you, and says that small worlds die. It is true, and no answer.

choices.text: Stop asking, and cure the flocks yourself

effects.log: It takes you a year and most of your faith. Oyun's flocks stand up in the spring.

choices.text: Write the pantheons a letter and sign it

effects.log: You sign it as a masterless god. It is read aloud, and laughed at, and remembered.

events.text: On the long road between pantheons you meet {ln_peer}, another god with no pantheon, who has been masterless for three ages and keeps a small domain of lost roads. {ln_peer} has a cart, a kettle, and a list of every small world the pantheons forgot. Lantern Hollow is on it, near the top, with a note: 'Oyun. Stubborn. Good.'

choices.text: Join {ln_peer} on the road for a while

effects.log: You ride the cart a season. {ln_peer} teaches you where the forgotten worlds are.

choices.text: Ask {ln_peer} why stay masterless

effects.log: 'Because nobody can tell me which worlds to forget,' says {ln_peer}.

choices.text: Share the kettle and go your own way

effects.log: A good cup of tea between two gods with nowhere to belong. You part as friends.

events.text: An envoy of {ln_order} comes to you at last, with a seal and a chair. The pantheon has heard of your small worlds and would like them in its ledger: you would be its god of the far star rivers, with a seat, a hall, and a leash, gently made of silk. Lantern Hollow would be a line in someone else's book. Oyun would never know.

choices.text: Refuse the leash

effects.log: You hand back the seal. The envoy is not angry; the envoy has seen this before, and envies it.

choices.text: Ask the envoy for the terms in writing

effects.log: The terms are long. Lantern Hollow is on page forty. You keep the copy.

choices.text: Ask {ln_peer} what to do

effects.log: 'Only you know what the leash is worth,' says {ln_peer}, and pours tea.

events.text: A domain of {ln_order}, the god of a great river world who once sneered that you had nobody, sends for you in a hurry. A drought has come to a corner of that river world the pantheon's ledger never mapped, and the only god who knows that corner is the masterless one who walks the forgotten worlds. The messenger is embarrassed.

choices.text: Go, and end the drought

effects.log: You end it in a week. The river god thanks you stiffly, and then, on the third try, warmly.

choices.text: Go, but ask to be named in their ledger

effects.log: You end the drought and are written in, as a friend, not a vassal. A first.

choices.text: Send {ln_peer} and the cart

effects.log: {ln_peer} goes, and does it, and comes back with a story the river god will hate.

events.text: Oyun of Lantern Hollow is old now, and the flocks are many, and the whole world prays to you by name each spring. Oyun asks, in a prayer, whether a god with no pantheon is lonely. Other small worlds have started praying the same name: worlds {ln_peer} told you about, and ones neither of you ever found. The pantheons still pretend not to hear.

choices.text: Answer Oyun in person, one last time

effects.log: You sit in the pasture with Oyun at sunset. You are not lonely. You both know it.

choices.text: Answer: a little, and that is all right

effects.log: Oyun sends back a song for the lonely gods. It rises past every pantheon.

choices.text: Gather the small worlds into a circle of prayer

effects.log: The small worlds begin to pray for each other too. It is not a pantheon. It is something.

events.text: They call you The God of Nobody's Pantheon now, half in mockery, half not. The small worlds pray to you, {ln_peer} keeps the kettle warm, and Lantern Hollow sends a song up the cold river every spring. At the Heavenly Court, {ln_elder} meets you on the stairs and stops, and for the first time steps aside to let a god with no pantheon pass.

choices.text: Pass, and nod as one god to another

effects.log: You pass. Behind you, the stairs are a little wider for the next god with nobody.

choices.text: Stop and ask {ln_elder} to walk with you

effects.log: You walk up together. The court does not know what to say, and says nothing.

choices.text: Go back down to the small worlds instead

effects.log: You turn back toward the cold river. The road is yours, and so are they.
